Prognostic Discussions
Valid: Nov 10 - 14, 2026 (6-10 Day Outlook)
Valid: Nov 12 - 18, 2026 (8-14 Day Outlook)
Issued: Nov 04, 2026
 
Prognostic Discussion for 6 to 10 and 8 to 14 day outlooks 
NWS Climate Prediction Center College Park, MD 
300 PM EST Wed November 04 2026 
 
6-10 DAY OUTLOOK FOR NOV 10 - 14 2026 
 
The 0Z ECMWF, GEFS, and Canadian ensemble mean forecasts are in fairly good   
agreement on the average large-scale circulation pattern over the North America  
domain during the 6-10 day period. While these ensemble mean 500-hPa height   
forecasts are generally similar, there are differences in the phase and  
amplitude of the primary features resulting in some variations in model surface  
temperature and precipitation forecasts. The manual height blend is based on 0Z  
ECMWF, GEFS, and Canadian model 500-hPa height forecasts, weighting the ECMWF   
ensemble mean (ECENS) greater due to recent model skill. The manual blend  
indicates a deep slow-moving trough from the Bering Sea across the Aleutians to  
the northeastern Pacific, with the easternmost extent of this trough reaching  
the West Coast of the contiguous United States (CONUS). Below normal 500-hPa  
heights are forecast over the Aleutians, Mainland Alaska, and Southeast Alaska.  
Anomalous ridging with above normal heights is forecast over much of the  
interior western and central CONUS. Meanwhile a mid-level trough is forecast  
off the Eastern Seaboard (its axis near 60W), extending southwestward across  
the Southeast.  Over the subtropical Central Pacific, a flat anomalous ridge is  
predicted which extends eastward across the Hawaiian Islands. 
  
Above normal temperatures are favored over most of the CONUS, due to anomalous  
ridging ahead of the deep trough forecast over the northeastern Pacific.  
Maximum chances of above normal temperatures range from 80-90 percent over the  
northern Plains and much of Minnesota. Near normal temperatures are indicated  
over New England and northern and central portions of Florida, on the back side  
of a mid-level trough forecast off the Atlantic coast. In Alaska, above normal  
temperatures are favored over the central and eastern Mainland, and Southeast  
Alaska, with chances exceeding 50 percent over Southeast Alaska. This is  
supported by the consolidation forecast, along with near normal temperatures  
for the western third of the Mainland. Well to the south, over the subtropical  
Central Pacific, the Hawaiian Islands are favored to be above normal, in  
proximity to a mid-level ridge. 
 
The positioning and strength of the cyclonic flow over the northeast Pacific  
Ocean promotes a stormy pattern across areas west of the Continental Divide,  
with above normal precipitation chances of 60-70 percent along the entire West  
Coast, and 70-80 percent from central California northward through southwestern  
Oregon. This is warranted by the consolidation tool, and by raw precipitation  
amounts from the GEFS, ECENS, CMCE, and NAEFS. It is consistent with the GEFS  
and ECENS Integrated Water Vapor Transport (IVT) tools which are used to  
forecast atmospheric rivers. To the east of the Continental Divide, above  
normal precipitation chances are elevated across portions of the southern  
Plains, Gulf Coast, and portions of the Southeast. This precipitation is due to  
increased return flow around a surface high pressure center predicted in the  
general vicinity of the Tennessee Valley, and also during the latter half of  
the period. In contrast, a mid-level ridge and associated positive height  
anomalies favor below normal precipitation from the Northern and Central Plains  
as far south as much of Oklahoma eastward across most of the Mississippi  
Valley, Great Lakes region, Ohio and Tennessee Valleys, most of the  
Appalachians, the Northeast, and the Upper Mid-Atlantic region. Chances of  
below normal precipitation reach a maximum of 60-70 percent along the northern  
tier states from the northeastern tip of Montana to Michigan. At higher  
latitudes, above normal precipitation is favored for northern, central and  
eastern portions of Alaska, based on the consolidation tool. There is a slight  
tilt in the odds towards drier-than-normal conditions over southwestern  
Mainland Alaska tied to offshore winds. A slight tilt in the odds for  
drier-than-normal conditions is also favored over most of the Hawaiian Islands,  
consistent with the automated and ERF-CON precipitation tools. 
 
The official 6-10 day 500-hPa height blend consists of 30% of Today's 0z GFS  
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 8, 40% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean  
centered on Day 8, and 30% of Today's 0z Canadian Ensemble Mean centered on Day  
8  
  
 
FORECAST CONFIDENCE FOR THE 6-10 DAY PERIOD: Above average, 4 out of 5, due to  
fairly good agreement among today's model height solutions, offset by some  
differences among model temperature and precipitation tools. 
 
8-14 DAY OUTLOOK FOR NOV 12 - 18 2026  
 
The 0Z ECMWF, GEFS, and Canadian ensemble mean solutions for the 8-14 day  
period predict a fairly consistent 500-hPa circulation pattern relative to the  
6-10 day period across North America and the surrounding regions, though with  
eastward progression. ECMWF-based tools were generally weighted more in the  
forecast, due to greater skill and persistence of yesterdays forecast. However,  
uncertainty increases in the forecasts for several areas of the domain. The  
8-14 day manual blend 500-hPa height pattern shows a deep trough and negative  
500-hPa height anomalies over the northeastern Pacific and the West Coast  
states. Residual cyclonic flow is forecast in its wake over southwestern  
Alaska. Downstream ridging and above normal 500-hPa heights are forecast over  
the north-central and interior northeastern CONUS. Farther to the south, weak  
anomalous troughing and weak below normal 500-hPa heights are predicted over  
the southeastern CONUS. Above normal mid-level heights are forecast to continue  
across Hawaii, associated with broad ridging over the central Pacific. 
  
Above normal temperatures are favored across the CONUS associated with  
anomalous ridging ahead of the deep trough over the northeastern Pacific. The  
highest confidence (greater than 80 percent chance) for anomalous warmth is  
indicated for eastern portions of the Dakotas and much of the Upper Mississippi  
Valley. This coast-to-coast warmth is supported by most of the dynamical  
temperature tools. Anomalous warmth is favored across central and eastern  
Alaska, due to east-southeast low level flow north of a surface low predicted  
over the Northern Gulf of Alaska. Near to below normal temperatures are favored  
behind this surface low, from the western Mainland to the Aleutians. Above  
normal temperatures are favored across Hawaii, underneath predicted above  
normal heights and consistent with expansive above normal sea-surface  
temperatures (SSTs) associated with the current El Nino. 
 
As the mid-level trough over the eastern Pacific slowly moves into the western  
CONUS, heavy precipitation is likely to overspread most of the western half of  
the Lower 48 states, with the greatest chances of 60-70 percent over western  
California and southwestern Oregon. Above normal precipitation is also favored  
across the Gulf coast and Southeast states, related to return flow around  
surface high pressure. Over portions of the Upper and Middle Mississippi  
Valley, Great Lakes region, Ohio and Tennessee Valleys, most of the  
Appalachians, the Northeast, and the Upper Mid-Atlantic region, below normal  
precipitation amounts are favored. This is related to the proximity of  
mid-level ridging and associated positive height anomalies. For Alaska, a mix  
of near to above normal precipitation is indicated. In Hawaii, the western  
islands (Niihau, Kauai, Oahu, and Molokai) are favored to receive below normal  
precipitation in week-2; while for the eastern islands (Maui, Lanai, Kahoolawe,  
and the Big Island), near normal precipitation is favored. This aligns with the  
automated precipitation forecast for Hawaii. 
 
The official 8-14 day 500-hPa height blend consists of: 30% of Today's 0z GFS  
Ensemble Mean centered on Day 11, 40% of Today's 0z European Ensemble Mean  
centered on Day 11, and 30% of Today's 0z Canadian Ensemble Mean centered on  
Day 11  
 
 
FORECAST CONFIDENCE FOR THE 8-14 DAY PERIOD: Above average, 4 out of 5, due to  
fairly good agreement among today's model height solutions, offset by some  
differences among model temperature and precipitation tools. 
 
FORECASTER: Anthony A 
 
Notes: 
 
 
The notation for the categorical forecast indicated on the maps is  
the same as that in the tables: A-above   N-near normal   B-below  
  
The temperature map shows regions with > 33% chance of being warmer 
(orange, "A"), colder (blue, "B"), or close to (gray, "N") normal. 
Labels on the shaded lines give the probability (> 33%) of the more 
likely category (B or A). Probability of N is always < 40%. 
  
The precipitation map shows regions with > 33% chance of being  
wetter (green, "A"), drier (tan, "B"), or close to (gray, "N") 
normal. Labels on the shaded lines give the probability (> 33%) of 
the more likely category (B or A). Probability of N is always < 40%. 
  
In the southwest and other climatologically dry regions - there will  
be a greater than 33.3% chance of no precipitation and occasionally  
even a normal (i.e. Median) value of zero - especially during the dry  
seasons.  In such cases a forecast of near normal is effectively a  
forecast of little or no precipitation.  
  
The climate prediction center uses 1991-2020 base period means as   
reference in the climate outlooks. 
 
The next set of long-lead monthly and seasonal outlooks will be released on  
November 19.
